END(paranoid_entry)

/*
 * "Paranoid" exit path from exception stack.  This is invoked
 * only on return from non-NMI IST interrupts that came
 * from kernel space.
 *
 * We may be returning to very strange contexts (e.g. very early
 * in syscall entry), so checking for preemption here would
 * be complicated.  Fortunately, we there's no good reason
 * to try to handle preemption here.
 *
 * On entry, ebx is "no swapgs" flag (1: don't need swapgs, 0: need it)
 */
ENTRY(paranoid_exit)
	UNWIND_HINT_REGS
	DISABLE_INTERRUPTS(CLBR_ANY)
	TRACE_IRQS_OFF_DEBUG
	testl	%ebx, %ebx			/* swapgs needed? */
	jnz	.Lparanoid_exit_no_swapgs
	TRACE_IRQS_IRETQ
	RESTORE_CR3	scratch_reg=%rbx save_reg=%r14
	SWAPGS_UNSAFE_STACK
	jmp	.Lparanoid_exit_restore
.Lparanoid_exit_no_swapgs:
	TRACE_IRQS_IRETQ_DEBUG
	RESTORE_CR3	scratch_reg=%rbx save_reg=%r14
.Lparanoid_exit_restore:
	jmp restore_regs_and_return_to_kernel
END(paranoid_exit)

/*
 * Save all registers in pt_regs, and switch GS if needed.
 * Return: EBX=0: came from user mode; EBX=1: otherwise
 */
ENTRY(error_entry)
	UNWIND_HINT_FUNC
	cld
	PUSH_AND_CLEAR_REGS save_ret=1
	ENCODE_FRAME_POINTER 8
	testb	$3, CS+8(%rsp)
	jz	.Lerror_kernelspace

	/*
	 * We entered from user mode or we're pretending to have entered
	 * from user mode due to an IRET fault.
	 */
	SWAPGS
	/* We have user CR3.  Change to kernel CR3. */
	SWITCH_TO_KERNEL_CR3 scratch_reg=%rax

.Lerror_entry_from_usermode_after_swapgs:
	/* Put us onto the real thread stack. */
	popq	%r12				/* save return addr in %12 */
	movq	%rsp, %rdi			/* arg0 = pt_regs pointer */
	call	sync_regs
	movq	%rax, %rsp			/* switch stack */
	ENCODE_FRAME_POINTER
	pushq	%r12

	/*
	 * We need to tell lockdep that IRQs are off.  We can't do this until
	 * we fix gsbase, and we should do it before enter_from_user_mode
	 * (which can take locks).
	 */
	TRACE_IRQS_OFF
	CALL_enter_from_user_mode
	ret

.Lerror_entry_done:
	TRACE_IRQS_OFF
	ret

	/*
	 * There are two places in the kernel that can potentially fault with
	 * usergs. Handle them here.  B stepping K8s sometimes report a
	 * truncated RIP for IRET exceptions returning to compat mode. Check
	 * for these here too.
	 */
.Lerror_kernelspace:
	incl	%ebx
	leaq	native_irq_return_iret(%rip), %rcx
	cmpq	%rcx, RIP+8(%rsp)
	je	.Lerror_bad_iret
	movl	%ecx, %eax			/* zero extend */
	cmpq	%rax, RIP+8(%rsp)
	je	.Lbstep_iret
	cmpq	$.Lgs_change, RIP+8(%rsp)
	jne	.Lerror_entry_done

	/*
	 * hack: .Lgs_change can fail with user gsbase.  If this happens, fix up
	 * gsbase and proceed.  We'll fix up the exception and land in
	 * .Lgs_change's error handler with kernel gsbase.
	 */
	SWAPGS
	SWITCH_TO_KERNEL_CR3 scratch_reg=%rax
	jmp .Lerror_entry_done

.Lbstep_iret:
	/* Fix truncated RIP */
	movq	%rcx, RIP+8(%rsp)
	/* fall through */

.Lerror_bad_iret:
	/*
	 * We came from an IRET to user mode, so we have user
	 * gsbase and CR3.  Switch to kernel gsbase and CR3:
	 */
	SWAPGS
	SWITCH_TO_KERNEL_CR3 scratch_reg=%rax

	/*
	 * Pretend that the exception came from user mode: set up pt_regs
	 * as if we faulted immediately after IRET and clear EBX so that
	 * error_exit knows that we will be returning to user mode.
	 */
	mov	%rsp, %rdi
	call	fixup_bad_iret
	mov	%rax, %rsp
	decl	%ebx
	jmp	.Lerror_entry_from_usermode_after_swapgs
END(error_entry)


/*
 * On entry, EBX is a "return to kernel mode" flag:
 *   1: already in kernel mode, don't need SWAPGS
 *   0: user gsbase is loaded, we need SWAPGS and standard preparation for return to usermode
 */
ENTRY(error_exit)
	UNWIND_HINT_REGS
	DISABLE_INTERRUPTS(CLBR_ANY)
	TRACE_IRQS_OFF
	testl	%ebx, %ebx
	jnz	retint_kernel
	jmp	retint_user
END(error_exit)

/*
 * Runs on exception stack.  Xen PV does not go through this path at all,
 * so we can use real assembly here.
 *
 * Registers:
 *	%r14: Used to save/restore the CR3 of the interrupted context
 *	      when PAGE_TABLE_ISOLATION is in use.  Do not clobber.
 */
ENTRY(nmi)
	UNWIND_HINT_IRET_REGS

	/*
	 * We allow breakpoints in NMIs. If a breakpoint occurs, then
	 * the iretq it performs will take us out of NMI context.
	 * This means that we can have nested NMIs where the next
	 * NMI is using the top of the stack of the previous NMI. We
	 * can't let it execute because the nested NMI will corrupt the
	 * stack of the previous NMI. NMI handlers are not re-entrant
	 * anyway.
	 *
	 * To handle this case we do the following:
	 *  Check the a special location on the stack that contains
	 *  a variable that is set when NMIs are executing.
	 *  The interrupted task's stack is also checked to see if it
	 *  is an NMI stack.
	 *  If the variable is not set and the stack is not the NMI
	 *  stack then:
	 *    o Set the special variable on the stack
	 *    o Copy the interrupt frame into an "outermost" location on the
	 *      stack
	 *    o Copy the interrupt frame into an "iret" location on the stack
	 *    o Continue processing the NMI
	 *  If the variable is set or the previous stack is the NMI stack:
	 *    o Modify the "iret" location to jump to the repeat_nmi
	 *    o return back to the first NMI
	 *
	 * Now on exit of the first NMI, we first clear the stack variable
	 * The NMI stack will tell any nested NMIs at that point that it is
	 * nested. Then we pop the stack normally with iret, and if there was
	 * a nested NMI that updated the copy interrupt stack frame, a
	 * jump will be made to the repeat_nmi code that will handle the second
	 * NMI.
	 *
	 * However, espfix prevents us from directly returning to userspace
	 * with a single IRET instruction.  Similarly, IRET to user mode
	 * can fault.  We therefore handle NMIs from user space like
	 * other IST entries.
	 */

	ASM_CLAC

	/* Use %rdx as our temp variable throughout */
	pushq	%rdx

	testb	$3, CS-RIP+8(%rsp)
	jz	.Lnmi_from_kernel

	/*
	 * NMI from user mode.  We need to run on the thread stack, but we
	 * can't go through the normal entry paths: NMIs are masked, and
	 * we don't want to enable interrupts, because then we'll end
	 * up in an awkward situation in which IRQs are on but NMIs
	 * are off.
	 *
	 * We also must not push anything to the stack before switching
	 * stacks lest we corrupt the "NMI executing" variable.
	 */

	swapgs
	cld
	SWITCH_TO_KERNEL_CR3 scratch_reg=%rdx
	movq	%rsp, %rdx
	movq	PER_CPU_VAR(cpu_current_top_of_stack), %rsp
	UNWIND_HINT_IRET_REGS base=%rdx offset=8
	pushq	5*8(%rdx)	/* pt_regs->ss */
	pushq	4*8(%rdx)	/* pt_regs->rsp */
	pushq	3*8(%rdx)	/* pt_regs->flags */
	pushq	2*8(%rdx)	/* pt_regs->cs */
	pushq	1*8(%rdx)	/* pt_regs->rip */
	UNWIND_HINT_IRET_REGS
	pushq   $-1		/* pt_regs->orig_ax */
	PUSH_AND_CLEAR_REGS rdx=(%rdx)
	ENCODE_FRAME_POINTER

	/*
	 * At this point we no longer need to worry about stack damage
	 * due to nesting -- we're on the normal thread stack and we're
	 * done with the NMI stack.
	 */

	movq	%rsp, %rdi
	movq	$-1, %rsi
	call	do_nmi

	/*
	 * Return back to user mode.  We must *not* do the normal exit
	 * work, because we don't want to enable interrupts.
	 */
	jmp	swapgs_restore_regs_and_return_to_usermode

.Lnmi_from_kernel:
	/*
	 * Here's what our stack frame will look like:
	 * +---------------------------------------------------------+
	 * | original SS                                             |
	 * | original Return RSP                                     |
	 * | original RFLAGS                                         |
	 * | original CS                                             |
	 * | original RIP                                            |
	 * +---------------------------------------------------------+
	 * | temp storage for rdx                                    |
	 * +---------------------------------------------------------+
	 * | "NMI executing" variable                                |
	 * +---------------------------------------------------------+
	 * | iret SS          } Copied from "outermost" frame        |
	 * | iret Return RSP  } on each loop iteration; overwritten  |
	 * | iret RFLAGS      } by a nested NMI to force another     |
	 * | iret CS          } iteration if needed.                 |
	 * | iret RIP         }                                      |
	 * +---------------------------------------------------------+
	 * | outermost SS          } initialized in first_nmi;       |
	 * | outermost Return RSP  } will not be changed before      |
	 * | outermost RFLAGS      } NMI processing is done.         |
	 * | outermost CS          } Copied to "iret" frame on each  |
	 * | outermost RIP         } iteration.                      |
	 * +---------------------------------------------------------+
	 * | pt_regs                                                 |
	 * +---------------------------------------------------------+
	 *
	 * The "original" frame is used by hardware.  Before re-enabling
	 * NMIs, we need to be done with it, and we need to leave enough
	 * space for the asm code here.
	 *
	 * We return by executing IRET while RSP points to the "iret" frame.
	 * That will either return for real or it will loop back into NMI
	 * processing.
	 *
	 * The "outermost" frame is copied to the "iret" frame on each
	 * iteration of the loop, so each iteration starts with the "iret"
	 * frame pointing to the final return target.
	 */

	/*
	 * Determine whether we're a nested NMI.
	 *
	 * If we interrupted kernel code between repeat_nmi and
	 * end_repeat_nmi, then we are a nested NMI.  We must not
	 * modify the "iret" frame because it's being written by
	 * the outer NMI.  That's okay; the outer NMI handler is
	 * about to about to call do_nmi anyway, so we can just
	 * resume the outer NMI.
	 */

	movq	$repeat_nmi, %rdx
	cmpq	8(%rsp), %rdx
	ja	1f
	movq	$end_repeat_nmi, %rdx
	cmpq	8(%rsp), %rdx
	ja	nested_nmi_out
1:

	/*
	 * Now check "NMI executing".  If it's set, then we're nested.
	 * This will not detect if we interrupted an outer NMI just
	 * before IRET.
	 */
	cmpl	$1, -8(%rsp)
	je	nested_nmi

	/*
	 * Now test if the previous stack was an NMI stack.  This covers
	 * the case where we interrupt an outer NMI after it clears
	 * "NMI executing" but before IRET.  We need to be careful, though:
	 * there is one case in which RSP could point to the NMI stack
	 * despite there being no NMI active: naughty userspace controls
	 * RSP at the very beginning of the SYSCALL targets.  We can
	 * pull a fast one on naughty userspace, though: we program
	 * SYSCALL to mask DF, so userspace cannot cause DF to be set
	 * if it controls the kernel's RSP.  We set DF before we clear
	 * "NMI executing".
	 */
	lea	6*8(%rsp), %rdx
	/* Compare the NMI stack (rdx) with the stack we came from (4*8(%rsp)) */
	cmpq	%rdx, 4*8(%rsp)
	/* If the stack pointer is above the NMI stack, this is a normal NMI */
	ja	first_nmi

	subq	$EXCEPTION_STKSZ, %rdx
	cmpq	%rdx, 4*8(%rsp)
	/* If it is below the NMI stack, it is a normal NMI */
	jb	first_nmi

	/* Ah, it is within the NMI stack. */

	testb	$(X86_EFLAGS_DF >> 8), (3*8 + 1)(%rsp)
	jz	first_nmi	/* RSP was user controlled. */

	/* This is a nested NMI. */

nested_nmi:
	/*
	 * Modify the "iret" frame to point to repeat_nmi, forcing another
	 * iteration of NMI handling.
	 */
	subq	$8, %rsp
	leaq	-10*8(%rsp), %rdx
	pushq	$__KERNEL_DS
	pushq	%rdx
	pushfq
	pushq	$__KERNEL_CS
	pushq	$repeat_nmi

	/* Put stack back */
	addq	$(6*8), %rsp

nested_nmi_out:
	popq	%rdx

	/* We are returning to kernel mode, so this cannot result in a fault. */
	iretq

first_nmi:
	/* Restore rdx. */
	movq	(%rsp), %rdx

	/* Make room for "NMI executing". */
	pushq	$0

	/* Leave room for the "iret" frame */
	subq	$(5*8), %rsp

	/* Copy the "original" frame to the "outermost" frame */
	.rept 5
	pushq	11*8(%rsp)
	.endr
	UNWIND_HINT_IRET_REGS

	/* Everything up to here is safe from nested NMIs */

#ifdef CONFIG_DEBUG_ENTRY
	/*
	 * For ease of testing, unmask NMIs right away.  Disabled by
	 * default because IRET is very expensive.
	 */
	pushq	$0		/* SS */
	pushq	%rsp		/* RSP (minus 8 because of the previous push) */
	addq	$8, (%rsp)	/* Fix up RSP */
	pushfq			/* RFLAGS */
	pushq	$__KERNEL_CS	/* CS */
	pushq	$1f		/* RIP */
	iretq			/* continues at repeat_nmi below */
	UNWIND_HINT_IRET_REGS
1:
#endif

repeat_nmi:
	/*
	 * If there was a nested NMI, the first NMI's iret will return
	 * here. But NMIs are still enabled and we can take another
	 * nested NMI. The nested NMI checks the interrupted RIP to see
	 * if it is between repeat_nmi and end_repeat_nmi, and if so
	 * it will just return, as we are about to repeat an NMI anyway.
	 * This makes it safe to copy to the stack frame that a nested
	 * NMI will update.
	 *
	 * RSP is pointing to "outermost RIP".  gsbase is unknown, but, if
	 * we're repeating an NMI, gsbase has the same value that it had on
	 * the first iteration.  paranoid_entry will load the kernel
	 * gsbase if needed before we call do_nmi.  "NMI executing"
	 * is zero.
	 */
	movq	$1, 10*8(%rsp)		/* Set "NMI executing". */

	/*
	 * Copy the "outermost" frame to the "iret" frame.  NMIs that nest
	 * here must not modify the "iret" frame while we're writing to
	 * it or it will end up containing garbage.
	 */
	addq	$(10*8), %rsp
	.rept 5
	pushq	-6*8(%rsp)
	.endr
	subq	$(5*8), %rsp
end_repeat_nmi:

	/*
	 * Everything below this point can be preempted by a nested NMI.
	 * If this happens, then the inner NMI will change the "iret"
	 * frame to point back to repeat_nmi.
	 */
	pushq	$-1				/* ORIG_RAX: no syscall to restart */

	/*
	 * Use paranoid_entry to handle SWAPGS, but no need to use paranoid_exit
	 * as we should not be calling schedule in NMI context.
	 * Even with normal interrupts enabled. An NMI should not be
	 * setting NEED_RESCHED or anything that normal interrupts and
	 * exceptions might do.
	 */
	call	paranoid_entry
	UNWIND_HINT_REGS

	/* paranoidentry do_nmi, 0; without TRACE_IRQS_OFF */
	movq	%rsp, %rdi
	movq	$-1, %rsi
	call	do_nmi

	RESTORE_CR3 scratch_reg=%r15 save_reg=%r14

	testl	%ebx, %ebx			/* swapgs needed? */
	jnz	nmi_restore
nmi_swapgs:
	SWAPGS_UNSAFE_STACK
nmi_restore:
	POP_REGS

	/*
	 * Skip orig_ax and the "outermost" frame to point RSP at the "iret"
	 * at the "iret" frame.
	 */
	addq	$6*8, %rsp

	/*
	 * Clear "NMI executing".  Set DF first so that we can easily
	 * distinguish the remaining code between here and IRET from
	 * the SYSCALL entry and exit paths.
	 *
	 * We arguably should just inspect RIP instead, but I (Andy) wrote
	 * this code when I had the misapprehension that Xen PV supported
	 * NMIs, and Xen PV would break that approach.
	 */
	std
	movq	$0, 5*8(%rsp)		/* clear "NMI executing" */

	/*
	 * iretq reads the "iret" frame and exits the NMI stack in a
	 * single instruction.  We are returning to kernel mode, so this
	 * cannot result in a fault.  Similarly, we don't need to worry
	 * about espfix64 on the way back to kernel mode.
	 */
	iretq
END(nmi)

ENTRY(ignore_sysret)
	UNWIND_HINT_EMPTY
	mov	$-ENOSYS, %eax
	sysret
END(ignore_sysret)

ENTRY(rewind_stack_do_exit)
	UNWIND_HINT_FUNC
	/* Prevent any naive code from trying to unwind to our caller. */
	xorl	%ebp, %ebp

	movq	PER_CPU_VAR(cpu_current_top_of_stack), %rax
	leaq	-PTREGS_SIZE(%rax), %rsp
	UNWIND_HINT_FUNC sp_offset=PTREGS_SIZE

	call	do_exit
END(rewind_stack_do_exit)

root_cause.rag: The vulnerability is an invalid pointer dereference flaw in the Linux kernel's aac_send_raw_srb function within the drivers/scsi/aacraid/commctrl.c file. This issue arises because the function does not properly validate a certain size value, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (DoS) or potentially have unspecified other impacts. The flaw can be triggered via an FSACTL_SEND_RAW_SRB ioctl call that executes a crafted SRB command. The vulnerability is present in systems with Adaptec RAID controllers support (CONFIG_SCSI_AACRAID) and requires full root-like privileges (CAP_SYS_ADMIN) for successful exploitation. The potential impact includes causing the kernel to dereference an invalid pointer, resulting in a kernel crash or possibly privilege escalation.

secure_coding_violation.rag: The vulnerable code block in the `aac_send_raw_srb` function does not properly validate a certain size value, which can lead to an invalid pointer dereference. This is a violation of secure coding practices as it involves unsafe memory use. Specifically, the function allocates `user_srbcmd` with a size based on `fibsize`, but later accesses it beyond this allocated size, potentially leading to a denial of service or other unspecified impacts. The lack of proper validation of the size value before using it to allocate memory and access elements is the core issue here.

The patch is available at the upstream repository: https://github.com/torvalds/linux/commit/07f12b26e21ab359261bf75cfcb424fdc7daeb6d.

score_explain.rag: The CVSS v3.1 metrics for the vulnerability indicate a base score of 4.7, classified as 'MEDIUM' severity. The exploitability score is 1.0, and the impact score is 3.6. The attack vector is 'LOCAL', meaning the attacker must have local access to the system. The attack complexity is 'HIGH', suggesting that successful exploitation requires specific conditions or circumstances. The privileges required are 'LOW', indicating that the attacker needs some level of access but not administrative privileges. User interaction is 'NONE', meaning the attack can be executed without user involvement. The scope is 'UNCHANGED', implying that a successful attack does not affect resources beyond the vulnerable component. The confidentiality and integrity impacts are 'NONE', while the availability impact is 'HIGH', indicating that the primary consequence of exploitation is a significant disruption of service. The CVSS v2 metrics also reflect a base score of 4.7, with an exploitability score of 3.4 and an impact score of 6.9, reinforcing the medium severity and highlighting the potential for complete availability impact. These metrics collectively suggest that while the vulnerability is not easily exploitable due to high complexity and local access requirements, it poses a significant risk to system availability if successfully exploited.

root_cause.rag: A double free vulnerability exists in the inotify subsystem of the Linux kernel before version 2.6.39. This vulnerability is caused by an incorrect fix for CVE-2010-4250, which introduced a regression leading to slab corruption by double freeing the `user_struct` in the `inotify_init1` function. The issue occurs when an error path in `inotify_init1` allows a normal user to trigger a double free of `struct user`, potentially causing a denial of service (system crash). The vulnerability affects local users who attempt to create files, and it is related to the cleanup process of inotify groups, where the user reference is not properly managed.

secure_coding_violation.rag: The vulnerable code block contains a potential secure programming violation related to memory management. Specifically, the code comments indicate a concern about hitting a "BUG" in the callback, which suggests a potential issue with the handling of the `idr` structure. The code performs operations on the `idr` structure, such as `idr_for_each`, `idr_remove_all`, and `idr_destroy`, without explicit checks or error handling to ensure that these operations are safe and do not lead to undefined behavior or memory corruption. This lack of validation and error handling can lead to unsafe memory use, which is a violation of secure coding practices.

mitigation.rag: The mitigation for the vulnerability is addressed in Red Hat Enterprise Linux 6 and Red Hat Enterprise MRG through the updates provided in the advisories RHSA-2011-0498 and RHSA-2011-1253. Additionally, the fix is included in the Linux kernel version 2.6.38.3. The patch corrects a double free/corruption issue of the struct user in the inotify_init1 function by ensuring that the user reference is properly managed when a group is cleaned up. The new lifetime rules for an inotify group are defined from inotify_new_group to the last fsnotify_put_group, ensuring that struct user and inotify_devs are only changed or updated in these locations. No specific system-level tools, kernel options, configuration files, or manual steps are mentioned. The mitigation does not explicitly state any limitations or side effects.

root_cause.rag: The coredump implementation in the Linux kernel before version 5.0.10 contains a race condition vulnerability. This vulnerability arises because the implementation does not use locking or other mechanisms to prevent changes to the virtual memory area (VMA) layout or VMA flags while it is running. This flaw allows local users to obtain sensitive information, cause a denial of service, or potentially have other unspecified impacts. The issue is related to the files fs/userfaultfd.c, mm/mmap.c, fs/proc/task_mmu.c, and drivers/infiniband/core/uverbs_main.c.

secure_coding_violation.rag: The vulnerable code block contains a secure coding violation related to improper handling of memory management and synchronization. Specifically, the code demonstrates a race condition due to inadequate locking mechanisms when accessing and modifying shared data structures. The function `uverbs_user_mmap_disassociate` iterates over a list of memory mappings (`ufile->umaps`) and attempts to obtain a reference to an `mm_struct` using `mmget_not_zero`. However, the code does not ensure that the state of the `mm_struct` remains consistent throughout the operation, as it releases the lock (`mutex_unlock(&ufile->umap_lock)`) before checking if `mm` is valid and returning. This can lead to a situation where the `mm_struct` is modified or invalidated by another thread, resulting in potential use-after-free errors or other undefined behaviors. The lack of proper synchronization and validation of the `mm_struct` state violates secure coding practices by allowing race conditions that can be exploited to cause denial of service or data corruption.

exploit_expl.rag: An attacker can exploit the vulnerability by leveraging concurrent modification of the number of VMAs, which disrupts the use of the heap-allocated array `vma_filesz`. Initially, `vma_filesz` is allocated based on the number of VMAs, and then filled by iterating over the VMAs and writing their calculated sizes into the array without re-checking against the array's size. The function then iterates over the VMAs again and dumps the entries in `vma_filesz` to userspace, without checking whether the array bounds were exceeded. This allows the attacker to leak in-bounds uninitialized values, leak out-of-bounds data, and write out-of-bounds data with constraints on what can be written. By using FUSE as a source of file mappings and as a coredump target, the attacker can pause the loops that perform out-of-bounds writes and reads, enabling them to write in the middle of newly allocated objects. The proof-of-concept demonstrates how this can be used to leak kernel heap data.

Exploit Code.portfolio:
elf_core_dump() has a comment back from something like 2.5.43-C3 that says:

        /*
         * We no longer stop all VM operations.
         * 
         * This is because those proceses that could possibly change map_count
         * or the mmap / vma pages are now blocked in do_exit on current
         * finishing this core dump.
         *
         * Only ptrace can touch these memory addresses, but it doesn't change
         * the map_count or the pages allocated. So no possibility of crashing
         * exists while dumping the mm->vm_next areas to the core file.
         */

However, since commit 86039bd3b4e6 ("userfaultfd: add new syscall to provide
memory externalization", introduced in v4.3), that's no longer true; the
following functions can call vma_merge() on another task's VMAs while holding
the corresponding mmap_sem for writing:

 - userfaultfd_release() [->release handler]
 - userfaultfd_register() [invoked via ->unlocked_ioctl handler]
 - userfaultfd_unregister() [invoked via ->unlocked_ioctl handler]

This means that VMAs can disappear from under elf_core_dump().


I see two potential ways to fix this, but I'm not sure whether either of them is
good:

1. Let elf_core_dump() hold a read lock on the mmap_sem across the page-dumping
   loop. This would mean that the mmap_sem can be blocked indefinitely by a
   userspace process, and e.g. userfaultfd_release() could block the task or
   global workqueue it's running on (depending on where the final fput()
   happened) indefinitely, which seems potentially bad from a denial-of-service
   perspective?
2. Let coredump_wait() set a flag on the mm_struct before dropping the mmap_sem
   that says "this mm_struct is going away, keep your hands off";
   let the userfaultfd ioctl handlers check for the flag and bail out as if the
   mm_struct was already dead;
   hack userfaultfd_release() so that it only calls vma_merge() if the flag
   hasn't been set;
   and because I feel icky about concurrent reads and writes of bitmasks without
   explicit annotations, either make the vm_flags accesses in
   userfaultfd_release() and in everything called from elf_core_dump() atomic
   (because userfaultfd_release will clear bits in them concurrently with reads
   from elf_core_dump()) or let elf_core_dump() take the mmap_sem for reading
   while looking at vm_flags.
   If the fix goes in this direction, it should probably come with a big warning
   on top of the definition of mmap_sem, or something like that.

#include <err.h>

#include <sys/mman.h>

int main(void) {
  // set up an area consisting of half normal anon memory, half present userfaultfd region
  void *area = mmap(NULL, 1024*1024*2, PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE, MAP_PRIVATE|MAP_ANONYMOUS, -1, 0);
  if (area == MAP_FAILED) err(1, "mmap");
  memset(area, 'A', 1024*1024*2);
  int uffd = syscall(__NR_userfaultfd, 0);
  if (uffd == -1) err(1, "userfaultfd");
  struct uffdio_api api = { .api = 0xAA, .features = 0 };
  if (ioctl(uffd, UFFDIO_API, &api)) err(1, "API");
  struct uffdio_register reg = {
    .range = { .start = (unsigned long)area+1024*1024, .len = 1024*1024 },
    .mode = UFFDIO_REGISTER_MODE_MISSING
  };
  if (ioctl(uffd, UFFDIO_REGISTER, &reg)) err(1, "REGISTER");

  // spawn a child that can do stuff with the userfaultfd
  pid_t child = fork();
  if (child == -1) err(1, "fork");
  if (child == 0) {
    sleep(3);
    if (ioctl(uffd, UFFDIO_UNREGISTER, &reg.range)) err(1, "UNREGISTER");
    exit(0);
  }

  *(volatile char *)0 = 42;
}

################################################################################

 One thing that makes exploitation nice here is that concurrent modification of the number of VMAs throws off the use of the heap-allocated array `vma_filesz`: First vma_filesz is allocated with a size based on the number of VMAs, then it is filled by iterating over the VMAs and writing their calculated sizes into the array (without re-checking against the array's size), and then the function iterates over the VMAs again and dumps the entries in vma_filesz to userspace, again without checking whether the array bounds were exceeded.
This means that you can use this to:

 - leak in-bounds uninitialized values
 - leak out-of-bounds data
 - write out-of-bounds data (with constraints on what can be written)

By using FUSE as source of file mappings and as coredump target (assuming that the system has the upstream default core_pattern), you can pause both the loop that performs out-of-bounds writes as well as the loop that performs out-of-bounds reads, so you should be able to abuse this to write in the middle of newly allocated objects if you want to.

The attached proof-of-concept just demonstrates how you can use this to leak kernel heap data because I didn't want to spend too much time on building a PoC for this.

exploit_steps.rag:
The exploitation of the described vulnerability involves the following steps and technical details:

1. **Environment Setup**:
   - The system should have the upstream default core_pattern.
   - Use FUSE (Filesystem in Userspace) as the source of file mappings and as the coredump target.

2. **Triggering the Vulnerability**:
   - The vulnerability is related to the concurrent modification of the number of VMAs (Virtual Memory Areas) and the use of the heap-allocated array `vma_filesz`.
   - The function allocates `vma_filesz` based on the number of VMAs, fills it by iterating over the VMAs, and writes their calculated sizes into the array without re-checking against the array's size.
   - The function then iterates over the VMAs again and dumps the entries in `vma_filesz` to userspace without checking whether the array bounds were exceeded.

3. **Exploitation Actions**:
   - Use the described race condition to:
     - Leak in-bounds uninitialized values.
     - Leak out-of-bounds data.
     - Write out-of-bounds data with constraints on what can be written.

4. **Proof of Concept**:
   - The proof-of-concept demonstrates the ability to leak kernel heap data.
   - The process involves pausing both the loop that performs out-of-bounds writes and the loop that performs out-of-bounds reads.
   - This allows writing in the middle of newly allocated objects.

5. **Files and Functions Involved**:
   - The coredump implementation in the Linux kernel before version 5.0.10.
   - Related files include `fs/userfaultfd.c`, `mm/mmap.c`, `fs/proc/task_mmu.c`, and `drivers/infiniband/core/uverbs_main.c`.

6. **Expected Behavior**:
   - Successful exploitation may result in leaking sensitive information from the kernel heap.
   - It may also cause a denial of service (system crash) or other unspecified impacts due to the race condition.

These steps and details are derived from the provided context and describe the technical process of exploiting the vulnerability without making assumptions beyond the given information.

The patch ensures that the mmget_still_valid() check is added to find_extend_vma(), preventing modifications to "mm" structures under mmap_sem for reading. This fix is applied to kernel versions before 5.0.10 and is related to files such as fs/userfaultfd.c, mm/mmap.c, fs/proc/task_mmu.c, and drivers/infiniband/core/uverbs_main.c. The issue is documented under CVE-2019-11599 and has been addressed in Red Hat Enterprise Linux 7 via RHSA-2019:2029.

root_cause.rag: An off-by-one error in the `build_unc_path_to_root` function in `fs/cifs/connect.c` in the Linux kernel before version 3.9.6 leads to a vulnerability. This flaw is caused by writing one byte past an allocated memory area, resulting in memory corruption. The error occurs during a Distributed File System (DFS) share mount operation when the server provides DFS referral names of a certain length. This memory corruption can cause the kernel to become unresponsive and crash, leading to a denial of service. The vulnerability affects systems with the Common Internet File System (CONFIG_CIFS) support and the feature to access Distributed File Systems (CONFIG_CIFS_DFS_UPCALL).

secure_coding_violation.rag: Off-by-one error in the `build_unc_path_to_root` function in `fs/cifs/connect.c` in the Linux kernel before 3.9.6. This error occurs when the code fails to correctly handle the pointer addition on `pos`, leading to a buffer overrun by one byte. The issue arises because the code does not account for the fact that `pos` has already been incremented by one when adding the length of `prepath`. This results in writing one byte past the allocated memory area, causing memory corruption and potentially leading to a system crash, which is a violation of secure coding practices related to memory safety.

root_cause.rag: A vulnerability exists in Ubuntu's implementation of overlayfs due to a failure to verify the ability of a user to set attributes in a running executable. Specifically, when Overlayfs sends the set attributes data to the underlying file system via `vfs_setxattr`, it fails to first verify the data by calling `cap_convert_nscap`. This oversight allows a local attacker to gain elevated privileges by exploiting the improper validation of file system capabilities with respect to user namespaces. The affected component is the overlayfs stacking file system in the Linux kernel, and the potential impact includes threats to data confidentiality, integrity, and system availability.

secure_coding_violation.rag:
The vulnerable code block contains a potential secure coding violation related to unsafe memory use. Specifically, the code uses the `copy_from_user` function to copy data from user space to kernel space without sufficient validation or error handling. This can lead to several issues:

1. **Buffer Overflow Risk**: The function `strncpy_from_user` is used to copy the user-supplied `name` into the `kname` buffer. If the `name` is exactly the size of `kname`, it results in an `-ERANGE` error, but the code does not handle cases where the `name` might be larger than expected, potentially leading to buffer overflow.

2. **Improper Memory Allocation**: The code allocates memory for `kvalue` using `kvmalloc` based on the `size` parameter provided by the user. If the `size` is not properly validated, this could lead to excessive memory allocation, which might be exploited for denial-of-service attacks.

3. **Lack of Comprehensive Error Handling**: The error handling after `copy_from_user` is insufficient. If `copy_from_user` fails, it sets `error` to `-EFAULT` and jumps to the `out` label, but there is no comprehensive cleanup or rollback mechanism to handle partially completed operations or allocated resources.

These issues highlight a lack of proper validation and error handling, which are critical components of secure coding practices.

root_cause.rag: A use-after-free vulnerability exists in the tcp_xmit_retransmit_queue and other tcp_* functions. The root cause of this vulnerability is that when tcp_sendmsg() allocates a fresh and empty skb and places it at the tail of the write queue using tcp_add_write_queue_tail(), it attempts to copy user data into this fresh skb. If the copy operation fails, the function undoes the work and removes the fresh skb. However, this undo operation does not revert the change made to tp->highest_sack, leaving a dangling pointer to a freed skb. Subsequently, tcp_xmit_retransmit_queue() can dereference this pointer and access freed memory. This condition can lead to SACK bugs or, with certain debug features enabled, crash the kernel. The vulnerability affects the Linux kernels as shipped with Red Hat Enterprise Linux 5, 6, 7, and Red Hat Enterprise MRG 2.

This action can trigger a use-after-free condition in the `tcp_xmit_retransmit_queue` and other TCP functions, potentially leading to a system crash. The exploit involves crafting a SACK option that causes the kernel to mishandle the SACK state after a failed data copy, allowing local users to cause a denial of service. The provided exploit code demonstrates the use of system calls such as `SYS_sendto` to send crafted data, which can lead to the vulnerability being triggered.

2. **Input Format or Payload Used:**

   - The vulnerability is triggered through a series of system calls:
     - `SYS_mmap` is used to map memory regions.
     - `SYS_socket` is used to create a socket.
     - `SYS_bind` binds the socket to an address.
     - `SYS_sendto` sends data to a socket.
     - `SYS_setsockopt` sets options on the socket.
     - `SYS_dup` duplicates a file descriptor.
     - `SYS_sendmsg` sends a message on a socket.
     - `SYS_recvfrom` receives a message from a socket.

4. **Expected Behavior that Confirms Successful Exploitation:**
   - The exploit aims to cause a use-after-free condition in the `tcp_xmit_retransmit_queue` or other `tcp_*` functions.
   - Successful exploitation may result in the ability to send an incorrect selective acknowledgment to existing connections, potentially resetting a connection.
   - The presence of a KASAN (Kernel Address Sanitizer) report or other debugging output indicating a use-after-free condition would confirm successful exploitation.

This can occur because `btrfs_rm_device()` may receive a NULL `device_path`, and calling `strcmp()` on it without checking for NULL first leads to a NULL pointer dereference. This violation of secure coding practices can result in system crashes or leakage of kernel internal information, impacting system availability. The fix involves ensuring that `device_path` is not NULL before calling `strcmp()`.

This vulnerability is caused by unexpected locking behavior, which allows an attacker to inject a malicious payload. The issue arises when the sco_conn structure, which contains pointers to previous data, is freed while still being accessed, leading to a use-after-free condition. Specifically, the code does not properly manage the lifecycle of memory objects, leading to a situation where memory is accessed after it has been freed. This can allow an attacker to inject a malicious payload, potentially leading to arbitrary code execution or denial of service. Proper synchronization and memory management techniques should be employed to prevent such vulnerabilities.

The bug occurs because the timer instance is incorrectly stored in `snd_timer_open()` even if the function returns an error. This is due to the misuse of the `timeri` variable, which is supposed to be the newly created instance but is used temporarily before the actual creation of a timer instance. This vulnerability can be triggered by a local attacker and may result in a denial of service (system crash) or possibly allow the execution of arbitrary code.

This leads to a situation where the `timeri` variable, which is supposed to be a newly created instance, is used for a temporary check before the actual creation of a timer instance. If the maximum number of instances is exceeded, the function should bail out, but due to the refactoring, it jumps to the unified error path and stores the `timeri` variable even when an error is returned. root_cause.rag: A flaw was found in the way the Linux kernel's `kvm_iommu_map_pages()` function handled IOMMU mapping failures. The vulnerability is caused by an incorrect third parameter in the `kvm_iommu_put_pages` function, which should be 'gfn - slot->base_gfn'. The issue arises when a malicious guest or userspace causes the function to pass a huge value as size, leading to a local denial of service (DOS) through host memory leak or memory corruption. The vulnerability affects the KVM (Kernel Virtual Machine) subsystem in the Linux kernel, specifically in the page handling logic.

secure_coding_violation.rag: The vulnerable code block contains a secure coding violation related to unsafe memory use. The issue arises from the potential for a malicious guest or userspace to manipulate the `gfn` value, causing the function `kvm_iommu_put_pages` to receive an incorrect third parameter. This can result in either a large value being passed, leading to unpinning of pages that should remain pinned (allowing unauthorized memory access), or a small value that causes pages to be pinned without being unpinned, leading to a memory leak. The lack of proper validation and error handling for these conditions violates secure coding practices by allowing unsafe memory operations and potential exploitation.

Patch code.rag:
```c
vm: add vm_iomap_memory() helper function

Various drivers end up replicating the code to mmap() their memory
buffers into user space, and our core memory remapping function may be
very flexible but it is unnecessarily complicated for the common cases
to use.

Our internal VM uses pfn's ("page frame numbers") which simplifies
things for the VM, and allows us to pass physical addresses around in a
denser and more efficient format than passing a "phys_addr_t" around,
and having to shift it up and down by the page size.  But it just means
that drivers end up doing that shifting instead at the interface level.

It also means that drivers end up mucking around with internal VM things
like the vma details (vm_pgoff, vm_start/end) way more than they really
need to.

The code uses `memdup_user_nul` to duplicate user data into kernel space, but it does not adequately verify the size or content of the data being copied, which could lead to buffer overflows or other memory-related vulnerabilities. Additionally, the function does not ensure that the user data is properly sanitized before use, which could result in privilege escalation or unauthorized access to system resources.

created, one per direction, and they are sorted differently.

In map_write(), at first, during the loop that calls insert_extent(), the member
lower_first of each struct uid_gid_extent contains an ID in the parent
namespace. Later, map_id_range_down() is used in a loop to replace these IDs in
the parent namespace with kernel IDs.

The problem is that, when the two sorted arrays are used, the new code omits the
ID transformation for the kernel->namespaced mapping; only the
namespaced->kernel mapping is transformed appropriately.

This means that if you first, from the init namespace, create a user namespace
NS1 with the following uid_map:

    0 100000 1000

and then, from NS1, create a nested user namespace NS2 with the following
uid_map:

    0 0 1
    1 1 1
    2 2 1
    3 3 1
    4 4 1
    5 5 995

then make_kuid(NS2, ...) will work properly, but from_kuid(NS2) will be an
identity mapping for UIDs in the range 0..1000.

Most users of from_kuid() are relatively boring, but kuid_has_mapping() is used
in inode_owner_or_capable() and privileged_wrt_inode_uidgid(); so you can abuse
this to gain the ability to override DAC security controls on files whose IDs
aren't mapped in your namespace.


To test this, I installed the "uidmap" package in a Ubuntu 18.04 VM with the
following /etc/subuid and /etc/subgid:

user@ubuntu-18-04-vm:~$ cat /etc/subuid
user:100000:65536
user2:165536:65536
user3:231072:65536
user@ubuntu-18-04-vm:~$ cat /etc/subgid
user:100000:65536
user2:165536:65536
user3:231072:65536
user@ubuntu-18-04-vm:~$


Then, as the user "user", I compiled the two attached helpers (subuid_shell.c
and subshell.c):

user@ubuntu-18-04-vm:~/userns_4_15$ gcc -o subuid_shell subuid_shell.c
user@ubuntu-18-04-vm:~/userns_4_15$ gcc -o subshell subshell.c

subuid_shell.c uses the newuidmap helper to set up a namespace that maps 1000
UIDs starting at 100000 to the namespaced UID 0; subshell.c requires namespaced
CAP_SYS_ADMIN and creates a user namespace that maps UIDs 0-999, using six
extents.

From 20598025d5e80f26a0c4306ebeca14b31539bd97 Mon Sep 17 00:00:00 2001
From: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Date: Mon, 5 Nov 2018 20:55:09 +0100
Subject: [PATCH] userns: also map extents in the reverse map to kernel IDs

The current logic first clones the extent array and sorts both copies, then
maps the lower IDs of the forward mapping into the lower namespace, but
doesn't map the lower IDs of the reverse mapping.

This means that code in a nested user namespace with >5 extents will see
incorrect IDs. It also breaks some access checks, like
inode_owner_or_capable() and privileged_wrt_inode_uidgid(), so a process
can incorrectly appear to be capable relative to an inode.

To fix it, we have to make sure that the "lower_first" members of extents
in both arrays are translated; and we have to make sure that the reverse
map is sorted *after* the translation (since otherwise the translation can
break the sorting).

This is CVE-2018-18955.

Fixes: 6397fac4915a ("userns: bump idmap limits to 340")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>

The issue arises when the user-defined length in the SNMP ioctl request is not properly checked against the size of the qeth command buffer, allowing local users to cause a denial of service or potentially have unspecified other impacts. This vulnerability specifically affects the s390x architecture and is present when the Linux kernel is built with Gigabit Ethernet device support (CONFIG_QETH).

secure_coding_violation.rag: The vulnerable code block contains a buffer overflow vulnerability. The function `qeth_snmp_command` does not adequately validate the length of the user-supplied data before using it to allocate memory and copy data. Specifically, the `req_len` variable, which is derived from user input, is used to determine the size of the memory allocation for `ureq` without checking if this length is compatible with the command-buffer size. This lack of validation can lead to a buffer overflow, allowing local users to cause a denial of service or potentially escalate privileges.

mitigation.rag: Check user-defined length in SNMP ioctl request and allow request only if it fits into a qeth command buffer.

root_cause.rag: Multiple off-by-one errors in the ext4 subsystem in the Linux kernel before version 3.0-rc5 allow local users to cause a denial of service (BUG_ON and system crash). This vulnerability is triggered by accessing a sparse file in extent format with a write operation involving a block number corresponding to the largest possible 32-bit unsigned integer. The issue occurs when an extent includes the block right before the maximum file offset, and the block for the maximum file offset is written, leading to a kernel panic. This problem is architecture-dependent, occurring on x86_64 for 4KB block sizes and on both i386 and x86_64 for 1KB or 2KB block sizes.

This indicates a violation of secure coding practices related to boundary checking and error handling. Specifically, the code fails to properly handle edge cases involving maximum file offsets, leading to potential system crashes. Additionally, the use of `BUG_ON` for error handling is unsafe as it can lead to kernel panics, which is not a secure practice. Proper validation and error handling mechanisms should be implemented to prevent such vulnerabilities.

root_cause.rag: A race condition occurs between `bcm_release()` and `bcm_rx_handler()`. When a message is received in `bcm_rx_handler()`, the socket can be closed in `bcm_release()`, which will free the `struct bcm_sock` and `struct bcm_op`. This leads to various use-after-free vulnerabilities in `bcm_rx_handler()` and, depending on the provided flags, also in `bcm_rx_timeout_handler()`. The use-after-free vulnerabilities, in combination with a heap spray, may lead to sensitive socket data being overwritten, resulting in local privilege escalation.

root_cause.rag: The vulnerability is a flaw in the Linux kernel's dl2k network driver's handling of ioctls, specifically in the rio_ioctl function in drivers/net/ethernet/dlink/dl2k.c. This function does not restrict access to the SIOCSMIIREG command, which allows local users to write data to an Ethernet adapter via an ioctl call. The root cause of the vulnerability is the lack of access restriction to the SIOCSMIIREG command. This vulnerability can be triggered by an unprivileged local user, potentially leading to a denial of service.

secure_coding_violation.rag: The violation of secure coding practices found in the vulnerable code block is related to the handling of the SIOCSMIIREG command in the `rio_ioctl` function within the `drivers/net/ethernet/dlink/dl2k.c` file of the Linux kernel. The code does not restrict access to this command, which allows local users to write data to an Ethernet adapter via an ioctl call. This lack of access restriction constitutes a secure coding violation as it permits unauthorized users to perform potentially harmful operations on the network driver, leading to a denial of service.

mitigation.rag:
The mitigation steps explicitly mentioned in the context are as follows:

- The patch removes all but the MII ioctls, renumbers them to use the standard ones, and adds the proper permission check for SIOCSMIIREG.
- The dl2k-specific struct mii_data is replaced with the generic struct mii_ioctl_data.
- The SIOCGMIIPHY ioctl is added since the phyid is available.
- The patch suggests that most of the MII code for the driver could be converted to use the generic MII library, although this is not tested due to the lack of a device.

No limitations or side effects are explicitly mentioned in the context.

The patch was reported by Stephan Mueller and signed off by Jeff Mahoney and David S. Miller.

root_cause.rag: A concurrency use-after-free vulnerability exists in the Linux kernel's floppy driver, specifically in the raw_cmd_ioctl function. This flaw occurs due to a race condition that leads to the deallocation of raw_cmd, resulting in a use-after-free scenario. The vulnerability can be triggered by a local attacker, potentially causing a denial of service (system crash) or possibly allowing the execution of arbitrary code. The affected component is the drivers/block/floppy.c file in the Linux kernel.

secure_coding_violation.rag: A concurrency use-after-free vulnerability exists in the Linux kernel's floppy driver, specifically in the `raw_cmd_ioctl` function. The issue arises because after deallocating `raw_cmd` in `raw_cmd_ioctl`, the `seek_interrupt` function still holds a reference to the freed `raw_cmd` and accesses it concurrently in `floppy_ready` or `start_motor`. This violates secure coding practices by allowing access to memory that has already been freed, leading to potential denial of service or arbitrary code execution.

root_cause.rag: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel's implementation of overlayfs. The vulnerability arises when an attacker opens a large file with write permissions on an overlay filesystem that is insufficient to handle the size of the write. This situation prevents the system from freeing an inode when unmounting the underlying device, leading to resource consumption. Repeatedly exploiting this flaw for all available inodes and memory can result in a denial of service condition.

secure_coding_violation.rag: The vulnerable code block contains a secure coding violation related to resource management, specifically a dentry reference leak. In the function `ovl_copy_up_locked`, if an error occurs, the function exits through the `out_cleanup` label, which calls `ovl_cleanup(wdir, newdentry)`. However, this cleanup function does not release the reference on `newdentry`, leading to a resource leak. The correct behavior should be to exit through the `out2` label, which ensures proper cleanup and release of resources. This oversight can result in a denial of service due to resource exhaustion, as the leaked dentry references are not properly released, potentially causing the system to run out of kernel resources.

exploit_expl.rag: An attacker with access to a developer account can exploit the vulnerability by running a crafted image in a container environment, such as Docker, where the runtime storage is on overlayfs over xfs. The attacker creates a large file within the container filesystem and attempts to read it, causing the xfs_file_open() function to return -EFBIG. This action can trigger kernel dentry leaks inside the container, eventually exhausting kernel resources and leading to a local denial of service (DoS). The process involves creating a large file in a lower layer and overlaying an upper layer that is too small, then inducing a copy-up by opening the file with write permissions. This results in the system being unable to free an inode when unmounting the underlying device, consuming resources and potentially leading to a denial of service.

root_cause.rag: A use-after-free vulnerability exists in the function io_sqpoll_wait_sq() within the file fs/io_uring.c in Linux kernel versions 5.10.y through v5.10.154. The vulnerability is triggered when the condition ctx->sqo_dead is not zero, which can occur by forking a new process and terminating it quickly. When the new process exits, the copied io_uring file descriptor is closed, leading to a call chain that includes io_uring_flush(), io_uring_cancel_task_requests(), and io_disable_sqo_submit(). In io_disable_sqo_submit(), the variable ctx->sqo_dead is set to 1. This vulnerability allows an attacker to crash the kernel, resulting in a Denial of Service.

secure_coding_violation.rag: The vulnerable code block contains a use-after-free vulnerability in the function `io_sqpoll_wait_sq`. The specific secure coding violation is the improper handling of the `wait` structure, which is defined with `DEFINE_WAIT(wait)`. The function uses `prepare_to_wait` to add the `wait` structure to the wait queue, but there is a potential path where `finish_wait` can be skipped if the loop exits due to a signal (`signal_pending(current)`). This can lead to a situation where the `wait` structure is not properly removed from the wait queue, resulting in a use-after-free condition. This violation of secure coding practices can allow an attacker to crash the kernel, leading to a denial of service.

exploit_expl.rag: An unprivileged local user can exploit the vulnerability by executing a bind system call for an RDS socket on a system that lacks RDS transports. This action triggers a NULL pointer dereference in the rds_ib_laddr_check function, leading to a system crash and denial of service.

exploit_steps.rag:
The vulnerability described can be exploited by following these steps:

1. **Environment Setup:**
   - The system must be running a version of the Linux kernel before 3.12.8.
   - The system should lack RDS (Reliable Datagram Sockets) transports.

2. **Input Format or Payload:**
   - An unprivileged local user needs to perform a bind system call for an RDS socket.

3. **Functions or Files Involved:**
   - The function involved is `rds_ib_laddr_check` located in `net/rds/ib.c`.

4. **Triggering the Vulnerability:**
   - The `rds_ib_laddr_check` function attempts to bind an address using `rdma_bind_addr`.
   - If the binding fails or the `cm_id->device->node_type` is not `RDMA_NODE_IB_CA`, the function returns `-EADDRNOTAVAIL`.
   - The function does not check if the device is NULL before dereferencing it, leading to a NULL pointer dereference.

5. **Expected Behavior:**
   - Successful exploitation results in a denial of service, specifically a system crash due to the NULL pointer dereference.

No additional technical details or payload specifics are provided in the context.

root_cause.rag: A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the `__nfs4_get_acl_uncached` function in `fs/nfs/nfs4proc.c` in the Linux kernel before version 3.7.2. This vulnerability allows local users to cause a denial of service, such as memory corruption and system crash, or possibly have unspecified other impacts. The root cause of the vulnerability is the accidental omission of a check for a too-small result buffer length in commit 1f1ea6c. When a `getxattr` system call is made for the `system.nfs4_acl` extended attribute on an NFSv4 filesystem, and the ACL has not been cached, if the buffer supplied is too short, the complete ACL is still copied, resulting in kernel and user space memory corruption.

secure_coding_violation.rag: The vulnerable code block contains a buffer overflow vulnerability. The violation of secure coding practices is due to the lack of proper validation of the buffer length before copying data. Specifically, the code does not check if the buffer provided is large enough to hold the data being copied into it. This oversight can lead to memory corruption and potentially a system crash, as the complete ACL is copied even if the buffer is too short. This issue is highlighted by the fact that the code attempts to copy the complete ACL without ensuring that the buffer length (`buflen`) is sufficient to accommodate the data (`res.acl_len`). This is a violation of secure coding practices, which require that buffer sizes be validated to prevent overflow and ensure memory safety.

mitigation.rag: This issue has been addressed in the following products: Red Hat Enterprise Linux 6.4 EUS - Server and Compute Node Only via RHSA-2014:0284 and Red Hat Enterprise Linux 6 via RHSA-2013:1645.

root_cause.rag: A flaw was discovered in the handling of routing information in the Linux kernel's IPv6 stack. The vulnerability is caused by the improper use of the DST_NOCOUNT flag, which should only be used if an authorized user adds routes locally. However, in the case of routes added on behalf of router advertisements, this flag must not be used as it allows an unlimited number of routes to be added remotely. This flaw can be exploited by a remote attacker to cause a denial of service through memory consumption by flooding the system with ICMPv6 router advertisement packets.

This is a violation of secure coding practices as it fails to implement proper resource management and validation, leading to potential resource exhaustion.

patch_expl.rag: The patch modifies the `net/ipv6/route.c` file, specifically the `ip6_route_add` function. root_cause.rag: A use-after-free flaw exists in the u32 network traffic classifier within the Linux kernel. The vulnerability is caused by the u32_change function, which, when entering an error path, mistakenly reduces the reference count of the current network namespace. This improper update of the reference count can lead to a use-after-free condition of the "struct net" data structure associated with the current network namespace. The issue affects Linux Kernel versions prior to 5.18, specifically from version 4.14 onwards. This flaw allows a local attacker to potentially escalate privileges to root, crash the system, or leak kernel information.

secure_coding_violation.rag: Improper Update of Reference Count: The vulnerable code in the `u32_change` function of the Linux kernel's u32 network traffic classifier contains a secure coding violation related to improper reference count management. When the function enters an error path, it mistakenly reduces the reference count of the current network namespace. This can lead to a Use-After-Free (UAF) vulnerability of the "struct net" data structure associated with the current net namespace, potentially allowing local privilege escalation.

The use of static variables `challenge_timestamp` and `challenge_count` without proper synchronization mechanisms in a multi-threaded environment can lead to race conditions. The attacker does not need to be on the same subnet as the target and can inject or take over a TCP connection between a server and client without executing a traditional Man In the Middle (MITM) attack. The exploitation can result in a denial of service by resetting the connection or injecting content into a TCP stream.

Function name.rag: hugetlb_reserve_pages(struct inode *inode, long from, long to, struct vm_area_struct *vma, vm_flags_t vm_flags)

root_cause.rag: A memory leak in the Linux kernel's memory subsystem (hugetlb) exists due to a flaw in the error handling path of the `hugetlb_reserve_pages()` function. Specifically, when called for anonymous (non-shared) mappings, the function allocates a `resv_map` but fails to release this allocation in the `mmap()` failure path because it performs a plain `unmap_region()` without invoking `remove_vma()`, which is responsible for calling `vm_ops->close()`. This oversight can lead to a denial of service by allowing an unprivileged local user to cause excessive memory consumption or a system crash through invalid `MAP_HUGETLB` mmap operations. The vulnerability affects the `mm/hugetlb.c` file in the Linux kernel versions before 3.4.2.

secure_coding_violation.rag: The vulnerable code block contains a secure coding violation related to memory management. Specifically, the function `hugetlb_reserve_pages()` allocates memory using `resv_map_alloc()` when called for anonymous (non-shared) mappings. However, it relies on the `vm_ops->close()` operation in `hugetlbfs` to release that allocation. In the event of a failure in the `mmap()` path, the code performs an `unmap_region()` without invoking `remove_vma()`, which is responsible for calling `vm_ops->close()`. This results in a memory leak, as the allocated memory is not properly released, leading to potential denial of service through memory consumption or system crash.

The exploitation involves calling hugetlb_reserve_pages() for anonymous (non-shared) mappings, which allocates a reservation map. The flaw is triggered when the mmap() failure path executes a plain unmap_region() without invoking remove_vma(), which is necessary to call vm_ops->close() and release the allocation. This sequence of operations allows the attacker to cause a denial of service by crashing the system.

root_cause.rag: The vulnerability in question is a logic flaw in the `mem_cgroup_usage_unregister_event` function within the `mm/memcontrol.c` file of the Linux kernel before version 3.2.10. This function does not properly handle multiple events attached to the same `eventfd`, which can lead to a denial of service through a NULL pointer dereference and subsequent system crash. The issue arises when a local user registers memory threshold events, potentially causing the system to crash. The root cause of the vulnerability is the improper handling of eventfd references, which allows for the possibility of a NULL pointer dereference when unregistering events.

secure_coding_violation.rag: The vulnerable code block contains a secure coding violation related to improper handling of multiple events attached to the same eventfd. Specifically, the function `mem_cgroup_usage_unregister_event` does not correctly handle the scenario where multiple events are registered to the same eventfd. When the function is called, it removes all events attached to the given eventfd. If no events are left, `thresholds->primary` becomes `NULL`. However, if the function is called again, it does not expect `thresholds->primary` to be `NULL`, leading to a potential NULL pointer dereference. This can cause a system crash, resulting in a denial of service. The violation here is the lack of proper validation and error handling for the state of `thresholds->primary`, which should be checked before further operations are performed.

The patch allows enabling STIBP (Single Thread Indirect Branch Predictors) with legacy IBRS (Indirect Branch Restricted Speculation) to protect against cross-thread branch target injection. This change is necessary because the IBRS bit is cleared when returning to userspace, leaving threads vulnerable. The patch modifies the logic in the spectre_v2_user_select_mitigation() function to exclude IBRS from the spectre_v2_in_ibrs_mode() check, allowing STIBP to be enabled through seccomp/prctl() or always-on if specified by the spectre_v2_user kernel command line parameter. Patch code.rag:
```
x86/speculation: Allow enabling STIBP with legacy IBRS

When plain IBRS is enabled (not enhanced IBRS), the logic in
spectre_v2_user_select_mitigation() determines that STIBP is not needed.

The IBRS bit implicitly protects against cross-thread branch target
injection. However, with legacy IBRS, the IBRS bit is cleared on
returning to userspace for performance reasons which leaves userspace
threads vulnerable to cross-thread branch target injection against which
STIBP protects.

Exclude IBRS from the spectre_v2_in_ibrs_mode() check to allow for
enabling STIBP (through seccomp/prctl() by default or always-on, if
selected by spectre_v2_user kernel cmdline parameter).

  [ bp: Massage. ]
```

root_cause.rag: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel's device-mapper subsystem, specifically in the dm snapshot facility. Under certain conditions, data written to snapshot block devices is incorrectly interpreted. Snapshots are constructed from a single "cow" (copy-on-write) device that contains a mixture of data and metadata. The bug involves a user writing a data block that is later incorrectly interpreted as metadata, which controls how blocks are mapped. This misinterpretation can lead to data corruption and allows an attacker to construct a mapping to read data from disk blocks in 'free space' that is normally inaccessible.

secure_coding_violation.rag: The vulnerable code block contains a secure coding violation related to incorrect handling of metadata and data allocation, which can lead to data or metadata corruption. Specifically, the issue arises when the function `persistent_prepare` allocates a new chunk and increments `ps->next_free`. If `ps->next_free` points to a metadata area, it is erroneously positioned, causing a newly-allocated chunk to be placed at the same location as the metadata area. This results in data or metadata corruption. The patch addresses this by ensuring `ps->next_free` skips the metadata area when metadata are loaded in the function `read_exceptions`. This violation highlights the importance of correctly managing memory allocation and ensuring that data and metadata are not conflated, which is a critical aspect of secure coding practices.

mitigation.rag: The mitigation involves a patch that addresses a data corruption issue when loading a snapshot's metadata from disk. The patch ensures that when a new chunk is allocated in `persistent_prepare`, `ps->next_free` is incremented and adjusted to avoid pointing to a metadata area. This prevents newly-allocated chunks from being placed at the same location as metadata areas, which would result in data or metadata corruption. The patch modifies the code so that `ps->next_free` skips the metadata area when metadata are loaded in the function `read_exceptions`. Additionally, a piece of code from `persistent_prepare_exception` is moved to a separate function `skip_metadata` to avoid code duplication. No limitations or side effects are explicitly mentioned in the context.

The patch message and code diff indicate that the length of the firmware string reported by the hardware can exceed the buffer size, leading to potential overwriting of memory. The patch addresses this by limiting the length of the data copied to the size of the buffer and using functions like `snprintf` to prevent overflow.

root_cause.rag: The vulnerability is a stack overflow in the Linux kernel's Transparent Inter-Process Communication (TIPC) protocol. The root cause is the failure to check that the `member_cnt` is below `MAX_MON_DOMAIN`, which defines the maximum size of the `members` array during initial sanity checks. This oversight allows an attacker to submit a malicious domain record with an arbitrary payload, which, if the `len/member_cnt` fields match up for the sanity checks, will be allocated memory. Subsequently, a newer domain record can be sent, causing the previous malicious record to be copied into a 272-byte local `struct tipc_mon_domain` `&dom_bef`, triggering a stack overflow. This vulnerability allows overwriting the stack contents following `&dom_bef` with the arbitrary members buffer from the malicious domain record, constrained by the media MTU.

secure_coding_violation.rag: The vulnerable code block contains a secure coding violation related to unsafe memory use. Specifically, the code uses `kmalloc` to allocate memory for `skey` without checking if the size of the allocation is appropriate or if the data being copied into `skey` is properly validated. This can lead to potential buffer overflow vulnerabilities if the size of the data exceeds the allocated memory. Additionally, the use of `memcpy` to copy data into `skey->alg_name` and `skey->key` without proper bounds checking further exacerbates the risk of buffer overflow, as it assumes that the data being copied fits within the allocated space. This lack of validation and bounds checking violates secure coding practices by potentially allowing an attacker to exploit the system through memory corruption.

mitigation.rag:
- Enforce configurations to prevent or limit attackers from imitating nodes in a cluster. Options include TIPC protocol level encryption, IPSec/MACSec, and network separation.
- `CONFIG_FORTIFY_SRC=y` is a hard mitigation for control-flow hijacking by performing a bounds check on the size of the offending `memcpy`, causing a kernel panic.
- Update the system to include the patch introduced in commit `9aa422ad3266` to mitigate CVE-2022-0435.
- Check if the TIPC module is loaded using the command: `$ lsmod | grep tipc`.
- Unload the TIPC module if loaded using the command: `modprobe -r tipc`. A system reboot may be required.
- Prevent the TIPC module from being loaded by adding the line `install tipc /bin/true` to the file `/etc/modprobe.d/disable-tipc.conf`.
- The mitigation may cause a kernel panic as a side effect when `CONFIG_FORTIFY_SRC=y` is enabled.

Additionally, a user-controlled pointer inside the 'struct ftrace_event_file' structure can be called through the ftrace_trigger_soft_disabled() -> event_triggers_call() function call-chain, leading to supervisor mode code execution of user-controlled code on systems without SMEP/SMAP-type protections enabled.

secure_coding_violation.rag: The vulnerable code block contains a secure coding violation related to the lack of proper boundary checking. Specifically, the `syscall_nr` variable is not verified against the upper limit (`NR_syscalls`) in the `ftrace_syscall_enter()` function. This omission can lead to an out-of-bounds read when the `test_bit()` function attempts to access non-present memory pages. This lack of boundary checking violates secure coding practices by potentially allowing access to unintended memory areas, which can result in a local denial of service (DoS) or aid an attacker in mapping the kernel address space layout under systems with kASLR enabled.

mitigation.rag:
This issue has been fixed with a patch in the kernel's mainline tree, specifically in the file `kernel/trace/trace_syscalls.c`. The patch ensures that the `syscall_nr` variable is verified against the upper limit `NR_syscalls` in the `perf_syscall_enter()` and `perf_syscall_exit()` functions. The relevant code change is:

```c
if (syscall_nr < 0 || syscall_nr >= NR_syscalls)
    return;
```

This change prevents out-of-bounds access by ensuring that `syscall_nr` is within the valid range before proceeding with further operations. The patch addresses the vulnerability by adding an upper boundary check for the `syscall_nr` variable, thus preventing the potential for local denial of service (DoS) attacks.

The issue has been addressed in the following products:
- MRG for RHEL-6 v.2 via RHSA-2014:1943

The issue does not affect the Linux kernel packages as shipped with Red Hat Enterprise Linux 5, but it does affect Red Hat Enterprise Linux 6, 7, and Red Hat Enterprise MRG 2. Future kernel updates for these releases may address the issue further.

root_cause.rag: The vulnerability in the Linux kernel before version 2.6.39 is due to the rose_parse_ccitt function in net/rose/rose_subr.c not validating the FAC_CCITT_DEST_NSAP and FAC_CCITT_SRC_NSAP fields. This lack of validation allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service through integer underflow, heap memory corruption, and kernel panic by sending data with a small length value to a ROSE socket. Additionally, a large length value in data sent to a ROSE socket can lead to stack-based buffer overflow attacks. The vulnerability is triggered when a remote host provides a length of less than 10, resulting in an underflow in a memcpy size, or a length greater than 20, causing a stack overflow of the callsign array. The affected components include the FAC_NATIONAL_DIGIS, FAC_CCITT_DEST_NSAP, and FAC_CCITT_SRC_NSAP facilities fields. The potential impact includes heap corruption and stack overflow, which may result in code execution.

secure_coding_violation.rag:
The vulnerable code block contains violations of secure coding practices related to the lack of validation for certain fields, which can lead to security vulnerabilities:

1. **Lack of Validation for Length Fields**: The function `rose_parse_ccitt` does not validate the `FAC_CCITT_DEST_NSAP` and `FAC_CCITT_SRC_NSAP` fields. This lack of validation allows a remote attacker to provide a length value that is either too small or too large, leading to potential security issues:
   - A length value of less than 10 can cause an underflow in the `memcpy` size, resulting in heap memory corruption and potentially causing a kernel panic.
   - A length value greater than 20 can lead to a stack overflow of the `callsign` array.

2. **Potential for Heap Corruption**: The code does not check against a maximum number of digipeaters (`ROSE_MAX_DIGIS`) when parsing the `FAC_NATIONAL_DIGIS` facilities field. This oversight allows a remote host to provide more digipeaters than expected, resulting in heap corruption.

These issues highlight the importance of validating input data, especially length fields, to prevent buffer overflows and memory corruption, which are critical violations of secure coding practices.

mitigation.rag: Check against ROSE_MAX_DIGIS to prevent overflows, and abort facilities parsing on failure. Additionally, abort facilities parsing when parsing the FAC_CCITT_DEST_NSAP and FAC_CCITT_SRC_NSAP facilities fields if a remote host provides a length of less than 10 or greater than 20 to prevent underflow in a memcpy size and stack overflow of the callsign array, respectively.

root_cause.rag: A vulnerability exists in the CAN implementation of the Linux kernel where a user with CAP_NET_ADMIN privileges can create a CAN frame modification rule that results in a data length code (DLC) exceeding the available CAN frame data size. This issue arises when a checksum calculation is configured to store the result relative to the end of the data, potentially allowing the tail of the socket buffer (skb) to be rewritten. This can lead to a system crash. The vulnerability is specifically related to the handling of CAN frames and the improper restriction of field sizes during the processing of outgoing frames.

secure_coding_violation.rag: The vulnerable code block contains a secure coding violation related to missing validation. Specifically, the code allows a privileged user with CAP_NET_ADMIN to create a CAN frame modification rule that can set the data length code (can_dlc) to a higher value than the available CAN frame data size. This lack of validation can lead to a situation where the tail of the skb (e.g., frag_list pointer in skb_shared_info) can be rewritten, potentially causing a system crash. The missing check allows CAN drivers to write arbitrary content beyond the data registers in the CAN controller's I/O memory when processing manipulated outgoing frames.

mitigation.rag: Drop frames that have a DLC exceeding the available space after the modification process. Limit the length for the checksum calculations to the maximum of Classic CAN data length (8). CAN frames that are dropped by these additional checks are counted with the CGW_DELETED counter, which indicates misconfigurations in can-gw rules. This mitigation is intended to prevent system crashes caused by a CAN frame modification rule that makes the data length code a higher value than the available CAN frame data size.

root_cause.rag: A use-after-free vulnerability exists in the Linux kernel within the function hci_sock_bound_ioctl(). The root cause of this vulnerability is a race condition that allows the hdev object to be freed while it is still in use. This can occur when userfaultfd is used to stop certain functions, allowing the detach routine to release the hdev object. After the hdev is freed, handling a page fault from copy_from_user() can lead to a use-after-free condition. This vulnerability can allow attackers to corrupt kernel heaps, specifically kmalloc-8k, and potentially adopt further exploitations. The vulnerability can be triggered by attackers with CAP_NET_ADMIN privilege.

secure_coding_violation.rag: The vulnerable code block contains a use-after-free (UAF) vulnerability. This occurs because the code does not properly handle HCI device detach events, leading to the potential use of a pointer to memory that has already been freed. Specifically, when the event `HCI_DEV_UNREG` is processed, the code detaches sockets from the device by setting `hci_pi(sk)->hdev` to `NULL`. However, if there are any remaining references to `hdev` elsewhere in the code, they may attempt to access this now-freed memory, leading to undefined behavior, potential denial of service, or arbitrary code execution. This is a violation of secure coding practices as it involves unsafe memory use, specifically failing to ensure that all references to a freed object are properly managed and invalidated.

root_cause.rag: A size_t-to-int conversion vulnerability exists in the Linux kernel's filesystem layer. This flaw arises from not validating the size_t-to-int conversion prior to performing operations, allowing a local attacker with user privileges to gain access to out-of-bound memory. This can lead to a system crash, leak of internal kernel information, and privilege escalation. The vulnerability is triggered by creating, mounting, and deleting a deep directory structure whose total path length exceeds 1GB, enabling an unprivileged local attacker to write the 10-byte string "//deleted" to an offset of exactly -2GB-10B below the beginning of a vmalloc()ated kernel buffer. The highest threat from this vulnerability is to data integrity, confidentiality, and system availability.

secure_coding_violation.rag: The vulnerable code block contains a secure coding violation related to improper handling of reference counts, leading to a potential use-after-free vulnerability. Specifically, in the function `aa_fs_seq_hash_show`, a reference is taken on the `profile` object using `aa_get_profile_rcu(&r->profile)`, but there is no corresponding reference drop before the function returns. This oversight can lead to a reference count leak, which may eventually overflow the reference counter and trigger a use-after-free condition. This violates secure coding practices by failing to properly manage object lifetimes and reference counts, which can compromise memory safety and lead to potential exploitation.

mitigation.rag:
- Set `/proc/sys/kernel/unprivileged_userns_clone` to 0 to prevent an attacker from mounting a long directory in a user namespace. However, the attacker may mount a long directory via FUSE instead; this possibility has not been fully explored.

- Set `/proc/sys/kernel/unprivileged_bpf_disabled` to 1 to prevent an attacker from loading an eBPF program into the kernel. However, the attacker may corrupt other vmalloc()ated objects instead (for example, thread stacks), but this possibility has not been investigated.

Important note: The mentioned mitigations prevent only the specific exploit from working, but other exploitation techniques may exist. To completely fix the vulnerability, the kernel must be patched.
